patches.title: NUL bytes in single-quoted strings
patches.origin: treebank; found by the first top-500 Packagist sweep

evidence.diagnosis: A single-quoted PHP string may contain any byte, NUL included, and symfony/polyfill-iconv's generated charset tables are full of them ('\x00' => '\x00'). tree-sitter reserves codepoint 0 for end-of-input, so NO grammar.js character class can ever match a literal NUL -- verified by trying: rewriting string_content's regex as /(\\?[^'\\]|\x00)+/ regenerates cleanly and still fails. Only lexer->eof() distinguishes a NUL byte from real EOF, and only an external scanner may call it. Upstream had already solved this for the contexts its scanner owns, which is why a NUL parses fine inside a double-quoted string, a heredoc and a nowdoc, and fails only in the three grammar.js-regex contexts: single-quoted strings, comments and inline HTML. The fix adds a STRING_NUL_CHARS external that consumes a run of NUL bytes, admitted inside string_content's repeat1 rather than beside it in `string`, so 'a\x00b' remains a single string_content node and the tree shape consumers query is unchanged.
evidence.scope_note: Only the single-quoted string context is fixed. The same root cause makes a NUL in a comment or in inline HTML fail, and neither occurs in the 86,308-file corpus, so neither is patched blind -- each would need its own external token and its own evidence.
evidence.evidence_note: 65 files, zero regressions: all 143 upstream corpus tests pass, and the before/after sweeps ran over the identical corpus with only this patch removed and restored.
evidence.upstream_status: not yet reported upstream; the patch applies directly to the pinned sha

patches.title: keywords as class constant names
patches.origin: treebank; found by the first top-500 Packagist sweep

evidence.repro:
<?php
class C {
    const mixed = 1;
    const MIXED = 2;
    const namespace = 3;
    const mixed TYPED = 5;
}
evidence.diagnosis: PHP accepts any keyword as a class constant name. Upstream already intends this -- _class_const_element uses reserved('nothing', $.name), which lifts the parser-level reserved-word restriction -- but that cannot help the type keywords, because they never reach $.name. PHP keywords are case-insensitive, so the grammar's keyword() helper compiles them to case-insensitive regexes, and /mixed/i beats $.name in the lexer for `mixed`, `Mixed` and `MIXED` alike. The token is then read as the constant's TYPE (typed class constants are PHP 8.3) and the declaration has no name left before `=`. The fix admits primitive_type and the namespace keyword in the name position, aliased back to $.name so the tree shape is unchanged; `const mixed MIXED = 1;` still parses as type + name.
evidence.measured_scope: The corpus only surfaced the SHOUTING_CASE spellings, because that is how constants are named, but the gap is general: before this patch every one of array bool callable false float int iterable mixed null object string true void namespace failed as a class constant name in lowercase too. Verified against php -l at both declaration levels, which differ -- in a class every keyword except `class` is a legal constant name, while at top level array/callable/false/null/true/static/namespace/list/print/echo/function are all rejected. Only the class-level rule is widened here; the top-level rule is left alone, so `const mixed = 1;` outside a class remains a (correctly narrower, though not exactly right) rejection and no corpus file needs it.
evidence.evidence_note: 10 files, zero regressions: all 144 corpus tests pass (143 upstream + this patch's), and namespace declarations, `use` statements, relative names (namespace\Foo::bar()), enum cases, property types, return types and parameter types were each regression-tested against php -l.
evidence.upstream_status: not yet reported upstream; the patch applies directly to the pinned sha

generate_cli_note: same pin as the other grammars: tree-sitter-cli 0.26.x ships broken Unicode identifier tables (see treebank-rust ledger). For php this pin also decides the upstream sha - see upstream.sha_note.
generate_dirs_note: both dialects are generated because both ship in the published crate, but only 'php' is loaded for sweeps (see the Lang impl): 'php' claims file-types ['php'] in tree-sitter.json and 'php_only' claims none, because php_only parses a region already known to be code, for injection into a host language.

corpus.source: Packagist dist archives of the top packages by Packagist's own popularity ranking. The dist archive is the published source tree Composer itself downloads, so there is no source/build-output choice to make the way PyPI's sdist-vs-wheel forces one.
corpus.ranking_note: Packagist's 'popular' order is Packagist's own and is NOT a plain sort by the download count it returns alongside each package (symfony/deprecation-contracts at 914M ranks above symfony/polyfill-mbstring at 1254M). The download number is recorded per package as reported; the ORDER is Packagist's ranking, which is the same kind of editorial-traffic blend npm's is, and unlike crates.io's raw counts. Stated here so nobody reads rank as a download sort.
corpus.url_note: Packagist states dist URLs as api.github.com/repos/<o>/<r>/zipball/<ref>, which allows 60 unauthenticated requests an hour - a 500-package fetch exhausts that in the first minute. resolve() rewrites them to codeload.github.com/<o>/<r>/tar.gz/<ref>, which needs no token and serves the single-top-level-directory tarball the fetch driver already strips. Measured over a sample of the top 500, every dist URL was on api.github.com; anything else passes through untouched.
corpus.files_note: .php only, the single extension tree-sitter-php's tree-sitter.json claims for the grammar we load. .phtml/.php4 are the same syntax and this grammar would parse them; they are excluded so classify() matches what the grammar advertises. Paths containing a vendor/ component are excluded for the reason javascript excludes bundles: it is Composer's install directory, so a failure there is attributed to the wrong package and the same code is already in the corpus under its real owner.
corpus.oracle: php -n -d short_open_tag=0 -l - the reference implementation's own syntax-check mode. TWO-VALUED: valid / invalid. Verified parse-only and non-executing: a file whose top level writes to disk and echoes produced no side effect, no output and exit 0; a missing require, an undefined base class and an undefined interface are all accepted, so each file is judged entirely on its own text.
corpus.oracle_flags_note: -n ignores php.ini so the box's configuration cannot move a verdict. short_open_tag genuinely can: with it on, '<? function f( { ?>' is a parse error; with it off the same bytes are inline HTML and the file is valid. It is pinned explicitly to the language default rather than left unset so a future change to that default cannot move the numbers. Measured bonus: -n also skips loading the ini's extensions, 35% of per-file cost (0.94 -> 0.61 ms/file), with zero verdict changes across 1703 files.
corpus.oracle_exit_note: 255 is 'syntax error'; 1 is 'could not open input file'. exec_oracle::run is told 255 explicitly and treats any other non-zero status as an ORACLE FAILURE rather than a verdict, because collapsing them would let a mistyped corpus root mark every file invalid, record every failure as noise, drop gap_files to zero and report a flawless grammar.
corpus.oracle_version_note: The interpreter version IS the language version, exactly as generate_cli is the CLI version, and for PHP it is not a formality. Measured on 1703 files from the top 40 packages: PHP 8.3.6 rejects 7 of them and PHP 8.4.23 and 8.5.8 reject none. All 7 are current Symfony, which declares 'php: >=8.4.1' and uses property hooks, asymmetric visibility and new-without-parentheses. On 8.3 those become corpus noise, so a grammar gap in 8.4 syntax would be silently discarded on the most-downloaded package family in the ecosystem. The Lang impl therefore REFUSES to run on anything older than 8.4 rather than answering dishonestly.
corpus.oracle_version_choice_note: Newest stable rather than a per-package version manager, because the choice does not exist: every one of the top 40's composer.json 'require.php' constraints is a FLOOR ('>=7.2', '^7.4 || ^8.0', '>=5.6') and not one names a ceiling, so the single interpreter satisfying all of them at once is the newest. Verified monotone within 8.x by probing 15 constructs across 8.3/8.4/8.5: each version accepts everything the previous one did and adds more; the only constructs all three reject ($s{0}, (real), (unset)) were removed at the 7->8 boundary, before every version in play.
corpus.oracle_cost: 15.4 s per 1000 files serially - 20x the next-worst Tier-A oracle, because php -l has no batch mode and forks an interpreter per file. Parallelized by exec_oracle at the machine's core count: 0.73 s per 1000 on 16 cores, a 21x speedup, flat past the core count (P=32 measured no better than P=16) and degrading gently rather than sharply under load (0.87-0.97 s with four other build sessions on the box).
corpus.oracle_batch_note: A batch oracle was built and REJECTED. opcache_compile_file() is non-executing, throws catchable ParseError/CompileError, survives duplicate declarations across files, and ran the whole corpus at 0.19 ms/file - 80x faster than php -l, and it agreed with php -l on all 1703 files. It is nevertheless WRONG: on a 22-file adversarial battery it silently accepted ten classes of invalid PHP (break/continue outside a loop, duplicate function, duplicate parameter, goto to an undefined label, reserved class name, misplaced strict_types, non-public interface method, duplicate default clause, new in a const expression), because the engine raises those as E_COMPILE_ERROR, which surfaces neither in the return value nor as a throwable nor in error_get_last(). Agreement on 1703 files of clean library code was worthless as evidence - only the negative battery caught it. A variant that scrapes the engine's own error log does match php -l on all 22, but it depends on diagnostic message text and buys a speedup the sweep does not need: validate() only ever runs on files the grammar already failed, which is tens to hundreds of files, where the parallelized php -l is already under a second. Recorded here so this is not rediscovered and quietly adopted.
corpus.packages_note: 500 requested; 499 resolved. roave/security-advisories publishes no tagged release (it is a metapackage of dev branches only) and the fetch driver skips it.
corpus.remaining_gaps_note: 6 gap files remain, in 5 distinct causes, each examined rather than left unnamed. (1) friendsofphp/php-cs-fixer PhpUnitTestAnnotationFixer.php and one other, failing at the very top of the file (<root> > ERROR(php_tag declare_statement comment namespace_definition ...)). (2) proxy-manager-lts Autoloader.php: `return (bool) require_once $file;` - a cast applied to a require expression, which the grammar's cast_expression does not admit. (3) league/uri-interfaces Converter.php: `return (string) match (true) { ... };` - a cast applied to a match expression; reported as a MISSING ';', which is the same cast-operand gap seen from the other side. (4) symfony/var-dumper Data.php: "\0$item->class\0$key" - the property name `class` accessed inside string interpolation, the interpolation-context twin of patch 0004's problem. (5) symfony/cache ValueWrapper.php: a class name containing a non-ASCII byte. None was patched blind: (2) and (3) are one fix and want a considered widening of cast_expression's operand rather than a quick alternation, and (4) needs the same reserved-word treatment inside the scanner-owned interpolation path.
corpus.noise_note: All 4 noise files are jetbrains/phpstorm-stubs, which describes PHP's own internals and therefore declares things no PHP file may declare: `class object`, `interface iterable`, `function clone(...)`, and a property on a class the stub redeclares. php -l rejects them and so does the grammar, which is the oracle agreeing with the parser rather than a gap - a useful sanity check that the adjudication is working.

grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.summary: tree-sitter-php parses syntax that PHP 8 removed, so for the cast case the grammar accepts a strict superset of what the oracle calls valid -- the same relationship treebank-python records for Python 2, and it needs stating because it decides what test/negative/ can contain.
grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.evidence: cast_type (common/define-grammar.js) still lists `real` and `unset`, both removed in PHP 8.0. Measured against php -l 8.5: `(real) 1` and `(unset) $y` are rejected by the oracle and accepted by the grammar. The other legacy spellings in that list -- binary, double, integer, boolean -- are still valid PHP 8 and agree. Separately, the grammar accepts `class C { const class = 1; }`, which php -l rejects because C::class is class-name resolution; this was verified against the pristine v0.24.2 tree, so it predates every treebank patch, and patch 0004 neither causes nor fixes it.
grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.why_this_is_safe: A sweep gap is 'grammar rejected it AND the oracle accepted it'. This asymmetry runs the other way -- grammar accepts, oracle rejects -- so it can never manufacture a gap and gap_files stays exact. For the casts it is upstream's deliberate support for older PHP rather than an optimization artifact; `const class` is simply an upstream bug.
grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.cost: test/negative/ cannot contain these three constructs, because the corpus asserts the grammar KEEPS rejecting a file and the grammar accepts all three. A (real) cast was written as a negative candidate, measured, and removed for exactly this reason. The 9 files that remain were each verified rejected by BOTH the oracle and the grammar.
